topic: Research: T3 Code Review 2026: Open-Source Control Plane for Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode

key_points: Frames T3 Code as a free, open-source desktop/front-end layer for AI coding agents rather than a model or agent runtime.
Highlights the unified-interface problem: developers split work across terminal agents, web apps, and cloud-hosted coding tools, losing workflow continuity.
Calls out practical workflow features: git worktrees for isolated agent work, built-in diff review, integrated terminal, and commit/push/PR actions.
Positions T3 Code as most useful for developers already using coding agents who are tired of context switching, while noting that provider support was still evolving when published.
Compares T3 Code against the official Codex app and argues the real comparison is interface/workflow, not model quality.
Gives T3 Code credit for Linux support, open-source inspectability, worktrees, diff review, and PR flow.
Raises a performance caveat via GitHub issue #695: one reported task finished in Codex in about 4m35s while T3 Code took more than 15 minutes.
Recommends starting with low-risk read-only tasks and using worktrees before trusting it with larger changes.
Places T3 Code in a broader 2026 AI coding harness comparison alongside Claude Code, Codex CLI, Aider, OpenCode, Pi, and Cursor.
Makes the important taxonomy distinction that T3 Code is not a harness: it is a UI wrapper over Claude Code and Codex CLI.
Warns that T3 Code depends on installed/authenticated underlying tools; without Claude Code installed, it cannot run Claude tasks.
Useful counter-positioning for the review: T3 Code should be judged as a control plane and workflow surface, not as the backend agent itself.
Reviews open-source AI coding tools and argues the differentiator is no longer only model quality because many tools connect to the same frontier models.
Emphasizes workflow fit, provider switching, context management, extensibility, and pricing/Claude subscription constraints as the real buying criteria.
Positions OpenCode as strong for terminal-first users and provider/model switching, giving the T3 Code review a natural contrast against terminal-first tools.
Surfaces the broader trend toward model-agnostic, user-controlled tooling rather than one-vendor coding environments.
Labels T3 Code an open-source control plane for orchestrating multiple AI coding agents, matching the target article’s core keyword angle.
Highlights unified agent orchestration, high-performance architecture, open-source/forkable design, and BYO subscription/credential control.
Targets software developers and open-source contributors who manage multiple agents or want to customize their coding environment.
The alternatives section is thin and partly generic, creating room for a stronger review that compares actual agent-control-plane tradeoffs.

stats.fact: The upstream T3 Code repository is pingdotgg/t3code, created on 2026-02-08, MIT licensed, and on 2026-07-10 showed 13,467 GitHub stars, 2,783 forks, and 676 open issues; the repo had been pushed on 2026-07-09.

The GitHub README says T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, and OpenCode, but users must install and authenticate at least one underlying provider such as `codex login`, `claude auth login`, `cursor-agent login`, or `opencode auth login`.
The README's quick-start path is `npx t3@latest`, with desktop installs also documented for GitHub Releases, winget, Homebrew cask, and Arch AUR.
The npm package used for the quick-start command is `t3`; npm listed latest version 0.0.28, published 2026-06-29, with 196 versions in the registry snapshot.
npm download counts for `t3` were 913 last day, 6,030 last week, and 22,068 last month for windows ending 2026-07-08.
GitHub Releases listed stable T3 Code v0.0.28 published on 2026-06-29; newer nightly release v0.0.29-nightly.20260709.769 was published on 2026-07-09.

T3 Code's architecture docs describe a Node.js WebSocket server wrapping `codex app-server` over JSON-RPC stdio, serving a React/Vite web app and translating provider runtime events into an orchestration model.

T3 Code's Codex provider guide supports multiple Codex accounts using a shared CODEX_HOME plus optional shadow home, enabling work/personal account switching while preserving shared session history when compatible.

T3 Code's Claude provider guide supports separate Claude homes for work/personal accounts and notes that switching Claude accounts inside an existing thread is usually not offered because different Claude homes are treated as separate environments.
SourceForge's mirror page listed T3 Code as a minimal web GUI for Codex, Claude, and OpenCode, registered 2026-06-25, last updated 2026-06-29, and showing 9 downloads for the week when fetched.
Community Q&A on AnswerOverflow summarized the OpenCode Desktop distinction: T3 Code drives Claude Code or Codex CLI under the hood, while OpenCode Desktop drives OpenCode CLI under the hood.

GitHub issue #695 reported a potential latency/performance gap: the same repository-investigation task allegedly completed in Codex in 4m35s but took more than 15 minutes in T3 Code under the same model configuration.

angles: Lead with taxonomy: T3 Code is an open-source control plane and workflow surface, not a model, not a replacement for Claude Code/Codex/OpenCode, and not a source of free inference.
Evaluate the control-plane promise through concrete workflows: project/thread management, worktrees, diff review, integrated terminal, PR flow, checkpoints, and provider/account switching.
Make provider dependency explicit: T3 Code inherits each backend's auth model, rate limits, subscription rules, CLI behavior, and outages, so the clean UI does not remove operational complexity.

Use the architecture as a differentiator: browser UI plus Node WebSocket server plus provider runtime ingestion is more than a skin, but the current architecture still appears Codex-app-server-centric.

Give a practical fit matrix: choose T3 Code for Linux/open-source/multi-provider UI workflows; choose first-party Codex or Claude Code for tighter vendor integration; choose OpenCode/Pi/Aider for terminal-first or more configurable harness workflows.

Address early-stage risk honestly: high GitHub interest and nightly velocity are promising, but hundreds of open issues, changing provider integrations, and at least one reported performance gap mean teams should pilot before standardizing.

Connect the article to the 2026 trend: agentic coding tools are converging on the same frontier models, so durable advantage shifts toward orchestration, reviewability, state management, and cost/control visibility.

Offer a unique reviewer checklist: install one provider, run a read-only audit, run a worktree-backed edit, inspect the diff, run tests in terminal, create a PR, then compare latency and trust against the same task in the underlying CLI.
